Structure-loss research · urban conflagration

Urban conflagrations as networks · 2026-10-13

Every building as a dot, linked to the buildings close enough for fire to jump between them. Three full records: Carlson 2002–22, our 2002–26 record and CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25, on the MTBS burned-area outline plus 100 m. How much of the loss spread house to house (every fire with at least 50 destroyed: Carlson 2002–22 135, Our 2002–26 record 155, CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25 51); whether Cat Fong's house-to-house push could carry fire through a town on its own; how destroyed buildings group from streets to whole towns; and whether the layout tells which buildings were lost.

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · 2026-10-18 15:05 PDT

1. Most destroyed buildings were lit by the wildfire itself. At most 28%–39% of the buildings destroyed (by record) were lost because a burning neighbour lit them; the share is about twice as high in fires whose largest block of close buildings held more than 89 (57% vs 28% in our record). 2. The house-to-house push alone is too weak to carry fire through a town. With Cat Fong's fitted push, fire could keep itself going from house to house only if the push were about 34 times stronger in the median fire (9–21 times even in the big urban fires): wind, embers and the fire front do most of the work. 3. Destroyed buildings form street-sized patches that join into larger burns. They join at about 125 m, much as the town's own buildings do, and not clearly earlier than a solid burned area of the same size: fire burns places, not scattered houses. From the layout of the buildings alone, neither density nor network shape tells well which buildings in a fire were lost (about 50 on a scale where 50 is a coin flip).
House to house: final-outcome contagion model with a spatially varying background (Sellke construction), fitted by approximate Bayesian computation on each fire's real layout, checked on simulated fires and a patchy-front trap. Network: single-linkage hierarchy of destroyed centres; spectral threshold ρ(P) < 1 for Cat Fong's kernel on 30 m groups of standing buildings; joining distance against chance patterns; fire-held-out per-fire AUC with fire bootstrap and Holm. Pre-registered verdicts: network adds to density — does not add; spread beyond network — does not add; spread alone vs density — does not add; merge ratio — has a preferred scale.

How to read this page

Plain words used on this page. Link distance: how close (centre to centre) two buildings must be to count as linked. Group: buildings joined by a chain of links. Patch: destroyed buildings linked at 30 m. Block: buildings standing before the fire whose centres are within 35 m of each other, chained; a fire's largest block is the predictor behind the 89 line. Urban conflagration: a patch of at least 50 destroyed buildings. Joining distance: the link distance at which a fire's separate groups of destroyed buildings join into one. Fire area: the MTBS burned-area outline (USGS and Forest Service) plus 100 m, or a public perimeter plus 100 m where MTBS has not mapped the fire yet; every number on this page uses it. Hover or tap any part of a chart for details; each panel has its own Plain / Technical switch.

How much of the loss spread house to house?

Of the buildings each fire destroyed, what share were lit by a burning neighbour, and what share by the wildfire itself? Estimated from the final loss map alone, fire by fire, for every fire with at least 50 destroyed in the three records, and tested on simulated fires whose answer is known.

Most destroyed buildings were lit by the wildfire; at most 28%–39% by a burning neighbour

Of all buildings destroyed in fires with at least 50 destroyed, the share lost only because a nearby building burned, estimated from each fire's final loss map: 36% in Carlson 2002–22, 39% in Our 2002–26 record, 28% in CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25. In every record the estimate and its range stay below half, so most destroyed buildings were lit by the wildfire itself. Read the dots as upper limits: a patchy fire front with no house-to-house spread (diamond) already gives a share nearly as large. The light band is the assumption range: the method has to assume how quickly the wildfire's own push can change across a town (the dot assumes about 200 m); if it can change over 100 m more of the bunching is credited to the fire front, over 400 m more is credited to neighbours.Pooled share = destroyed-weighted mean of per-fire posterior medians (background σ = 200 m, hole 100 m); 95%: 2,000 fire-bootstrap draws × one posterior draw per fire. Band: full re-runs at σ = 100 m and 400 m (200 simulations per fire). Diamond: median ABC estimate over the trap simulations (β = 0, background from each fire's own 50 m loss map). Pre-set verdicts: Carlson 2002–22: mostly lit by the wildfire; house-to-house is a real part of the loss; Our 2002–26 record: mostly lit by the wildfire; house-to-house is a real part of the loss; CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25: mostly lit by the wildfire; house-to-house is a real part of the loss; trap: fooled: shares are upper bounds; background scale: depends on the background scale (largest move 0.173). Outside checks (Waldo Canyon 2012, Lahaina 2023; not a record, not pooled): 63% of 2,242 destroyed.

How this panel was checked
  • Three full records, each with every fire that had at least 50 destroyed inside the fire area (MTBS burned area + 100 m); fire and building counts are printed on each row.
  • The dot weights fires by their destroyed buildings; the typical fire (each fire counts once) is in the hover. The largest single fire is Camp 2018: 24% of the destroyed buildings in Carlson 2002–22, and without it the share is 35% instead of 36%; 20% of the destroyed buildings in Our 2002–26 record, and without it the share is 40% instead of 39%; 30% of the destroyed buildings in CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25, and without it the share is 31% instead of 28%.
  • Ranges come from resampling fires, not buildings, and carry each fire's own uncertainty.
  • The 100 m and 400 m runs re-do everything (simulations, estimator, background) at that scale; they are not a re-weighting of the main run.
  • Upper limit, not a point fact: the trap simulations (no house-to-house spread) give shares close to the real ones in every record.

Lit by the fire front, or lit by a neighbour? How the share is estimated

In this made-up street: 13 of 21 houses destroyed; 6 of those 13 were lit by a neighbour.
lit by the wildfire (front, embers) lit by a burning neighbour survived

The question. When a fire reaches a town, some houses are lit directly by the wildfire and some catch fire from a burning house next door. Of the buildings each fire destroyed, what share were lit by a neighbour?

Why it is hard. We only have the final map of which buildings were destroyed and which survived, with no record of what burned first. Two burned houses side by side could mean one lit the other, or that the wildfire reached both.

What we count. A destroyed building counts as "lit by a neighbour" if the wildfire alone would not have destroyed it: it was lost only because a nearby building burned.

How. (1) For each fire, measure how much more tightly the losses bunch together at 10–50 m than the fire's broad pattern gives; the wildfire's own push may be stronger in some parts of the fire area than others, but changes only gradually, over about 200 m. (2) On the same fire's real buildings, simulate 400 fires that destroy the same number of buildings, each with a known share lit by a neighbour, from none to almost all. (3) Keep the simulated fires whose bunching looks most like the real fire's; their known shares give the estimate and its range. The approach comes from plant and livestock disease studies that work from a single final map of which places were infected.

Final-outcome epidemic with background infection (Sellke construction): Q_i ~ Exp(1); i destroyed iff Q_i ≤ α_i + β Σ_(j destroyed) exp(−d_ij/λ) (d ≤ 200 m); the final map is the minimal fixed point. Estimand: share of destroyed with Q_i > α_i (counterfactual: not destroyed by the background alone). Background α_i = c·b_i, b_i = −log(1 − m_i), m_i = Gaussian (σ = 200 m) share destroyed among buildings ≥ 100 m away. Kernel: exp(−d/λ). Estimator: pseudo-likelihood P(D_i | D_−i) = 1 − exp(−(a0 + a1 b_i + β S_i)), λ ∈ {10, 20, 30, 50} m; summaries: naive share and log(β̂ + 0.001). Snapshot correction by ABC: 400 simulations per fire on the real layout, λ ~ U(10, 50) m, β = 0 (p 0.1) or log-U(0.01, 20), c bisected to the observed destroyed count (within 25%), identical estimator; nearest 20% accepted, Epanechnikov weights, prior flattened to uniform on the share, local-linear adjustment on logit(share). Keeling, Brooks & Gilligan 2004; Demiris & O'Neill 2005; Kypraios et al. 2017; Beaumont et al. 2002.

How this panel was checked
  • Model, estimand, the 400 simulations, the recovery test, the trap test and every pass/fail bar were written down and committed before any number on real fires was computed.
  • The illustration is made up (21 houses); every number elsewhere in this section comes from the tables the analysis wrote.
  • 'Lit by a neighbour' means 'would not have been destroyed by the wildfire alone'. It is not the same as 'reached first by a neighbour' (what NIST counted at Waldo Canyon); ours is the smaller of the two whenever both could have reached a house.

On simulated fires the method finds a known share, but a patchy fire front fools it

On every fire's real buildings we simulated fires with a known share lit by a neighbour and asked the method to find it from the final map alone. It finds the share closely (typically 2–3 points off), but its 95% ranges held the truth in only 77%–79% of tests, so treat them as about 80% ranges. The trap (orange diamond) has no house-to-house spread at all, only a patchy fire front, and the method still reports 23%–31%: the shares on real fires are upper limits.Leave-one-simulation-out: 40 held-out simulations per fire, each estimated by ABC from that fire's other 399. Bars: bins of true share (10 bins). Pre-set bars: recovers if median |error| ≤ 0.10, r ≥ 0.80 and coverage 0.85–0.99 in all three records; trap 'not fooled' if median ≤ 0.15. Verdicts: partly recovers; trap: fooled: shares are upper bounds.

How this panel was checked
  • The simulated fires use each real fire's own building layout and its own destroyed count, so the test is as hard as the real problem, not an idealised grid.
  • Every simulated fire is estimated with the other 399 simulations only (its own left out), the same way the real fire is estimated.
  • Recovery is a necessary check, not proof: the trap tests the main way the model can be wrong (a wildfire push that changes sharply over tens of metres).
  • Bands with fewer than 5 simulated fires are not drawn.

Fire by fire: house-to-house spread shows through clearly in only 6 of 155 fires

Each dot is one fire with at least 50 buildings destroyed; the grey diamond is what a patchy fire front alone, with no house-to-house spread, gives on the same buildings. Most dots sit near their diamond, so for most fires the final map cannot tell the two apart. In 6 of the 155 fires of our 2002–26 record the share is clearly above it: Camp 2018, Almeda Drive 2020, Marshall 2021, Dixie 2021, Summit 2008, Mosquito 2022. The share is about twice as high in fires whose largest block held more than 89 buildings

Each dot is one fire. Across: the fire's largest block of buildings standing before the fire (centres within 35 m of each other, chained); up: the share of its destroyed buildings lit by a neighbour. In fires above the 89 line (no fire whose largest block held 89 or fewer became an urban conflagration in any of the three records) the share averages 57%, against 28% at or below it (our record). A patchy front alone also gives more in big blocks (48% vs 33%), so only part of the gap is house-to-house spread; this describes fires, it does not show a cause.Block = largest single-linkage group at 35 m between centres of the buildings in reach (MTBS + 100 m); 89 line = 89.09 (fixed in the definition work, not re-chosen here). Spearman and differences with 2,000 fire-bootstrap draws × posterior draws. Pre-set verdict: rises with block size.

Could the house-to-house push carry fire through a town on its own?

Cat Fong's contagion model links every pair of buildings with a push that fades with distance. On the real web of buildings we can ask whether that push is strong enough for fire to keep spreading by itself.

Cat Fong's fitted house-to-house push would have to be about 34 times stronger for fire to keep itself going

Cat's contagion model says each burning building nearby slightly raises a building's chance of burning (fitted push β ≈ 0.035, fading over about 12.5 m). Put on the real web of buildings, that push is far too weak for fire to keep going from house to house on its own: it would have to be about 34 times stronger in the median fire, and 9 times in Tubbs 2017, 13 times in Camp 2018, 21 times in Marshall 2021, 12 times in Eaton 2025, 21 times in Lahaina 2023 even in the most tightly packed part of the big urban fires. So urban conflagrations need the wildfire's help (wind, embers, many ignitions at once); house-to-house spread adds to the loss, as the section above estimates, but does not drive it alone.Cat's model as a network: P_ij = 1 − exp(−β K_ij), K = exp(−d/12.5 m), pairs ≤ 60 m, built on each 30 m group of standing buildings. A self-sustaining outbreak needs the spectral radius ρ(P) > 1 (Wang et al. 2003; Newman 2002). Max ρ(P) at β = 0.035 over all fires: 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.14 (three records). β_crit = 1/ρ(K) for each fire's most tightly packed 30 m group; median over 353 / 440 / 110 fires with ≥ 10 destroyed. Cat's β and λ were fitted to the residual distance-response in Carlson 2013–22 after adjusting for the wildfire (Fong 2026 briefing).

How destroyed buildings group: patches and groups of groups

Link destroyed buildings that stand close together and they form patches; raise the link distance and the patches join into larger burns.

Houses as dots, joined by lines: street groups at 30 m, groups of groups at 50–75 m (illustration)

An illustration, not a real town: 29 houses, 7 trees. Filled houses were destroyed; houses with a white dot survived. Drag the slider: at 30 m the houses on each street join into street groups; at 50–75 m nearby street groups join into groups of groups; past about 160 m the whole town is one group.Single linkage on centres: groups at distance d are the connected components of the graph with edges ≤ d, equivalently the minimum spanning tree cut at d. Burned groups join at about 125 m, close to where the town's own buildings join

The joining distance is the link distance at which a fire's separate groups of destroyed buildings join into one. In fires with at least 100 destroyed it is usually well above 50 m (median 125, 125 and 135 m in the three records), and in 107 of 109 fires of our record the groups join gradually rather than in one sudden jump. Destroyed buildings join at about the same distance as all the buildings of the town before the fire (median 135 m), so the joining distance mostly reflects how the town is laid out.Pre-registered verdicts: jump vs smooth — smooth climbs; vs town — the tipping point is town layout; vs random picks — burning is clumpier than chance at the tipping scale (only fires where random picks join inside 150 m enter; the censoring-aware sign test, exploratory, says destroyed joins earlier in 83 of 89 fires in our record); near 50 m — not near 50 m. Joining distance = argmax over d ∈ {10, 15, …, 150} m of the second-largest single-linkage component share; sub-sampling range from dropping 10% of destroyed buildings.

Destroyed buildings join up earlier than random picks, but not clearly earlier than a solid burned area of the same size

One dot per fire with at least 100 destroyed buildings. Up: the joining distance of the real losses; across: the same for a chance pattern with the same number of buildings. Shown first, a solid burned area of the same size: dots fall on both sides of the line (60 fires earlier, 31 later in our record), and at 50 m the real losses' biggest group is smaller (4.3% of the destroyed vs 7.0%). Switch to 'random picks inside the fire area' and almost every dot falls below the line (83 of the 89 fires that one side won): losses look far more clustered than scattered picks mainly because fire burns places, not scattered houses. Against picks that follow the fire's broad loss map the real losses clump a little more (76 earlier, 8 later), consistent with, but not proof of, spread between nearby buildings.Joining distance = argmax over d ∈ {10, 15, …, 150} m of the share in the second-largest single-linkage group of building centres; argmax at 150 m = not joined (right-censored, drawn at 165 m). Baseline curves are means over 20 draws. Two-sided sign test (ties dropped); Holm over the four main patterns × 3 records; Clopper–Pearson interval for the share earlier. Pre-set rule: 'clumps more' needs Holm p < 0.05 toward earlier and the fire-bootstrap 95% interval of the median paired difference in the 50 m biggest-group share above 0, in ≥ 2 of 3 records. Verdicts: solid area — about the same / can't tell; broad loss map — real losses clump more than these picks; headline — the original comparison mostly shows that fire burns places, not scattered houses. Biggest-group share lower than the solid area with the interval below 0 in 6 of 6 record × distance (50, 75 m) cells. How this panel was checked
  • Each fire counts once; the denominator is every fire in the record with at least 100 destroyed inside the fire area; ties are counted and shown, not dropped silently.
  • Fires that never join up within 150 m are drawn in a separate strip and never given an invented value.
  • The sign test uses only fires one side won, and the readout says how many fires that leaves; its interval is exact (Clopper–Pearson), so it stays within 0–100%.
  • The joining distance is a coarse measure (5 m steps, a single peak); the biggest-group share at 50 m, defined for every fire, is given in the caption and in each dot's hover.
  • The chance patterns and the rule for 'clumps more' were written down before any of these numbers was computed; the original comparison (random picks inside the fire area) was reproduced exactly first.

Each doubling of the link distance merges more groups than the last: preferred scales, not a fractal

A fractal pattern would merge groups at the same rate at every scale. Destroyed buildings do not: each doubling of the link distance from 30 to 480 m merges more groups than the one before, in all three records, and the town before the fire does the same. There are preferred scales: street groups below about 30 m, neighbourhoods at 50–300 m, then whole towns.Merge ratio N(d)/N(2d) of single-linkage components, fires ≥ 100 destroyed; per-fire slope of log ratio on log d; bar for 'self-similar': 95% interval inside ±0.10. Verdicts (pre-set): Carlson 2002–22: has a preferred scale; Our 2002–26 record: has a preferred scale; CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25: has a preferred scale. Related checks not shown: patch sizes are heavy-tailed but not a power law (heavy-tailed but not a power law); pair-counting dimension: destroyed pattern more clumped than the town; box counting: can't tell.

How this panel was checked
  • Fires with at least 100 destroyed only (fewer give too few groups to count); median fire shown, intervals from resampling fires.
  • The standing town (our record) is shown as the comparison: it also merges faster at larger scales.

All 8 named urban conflagrations were several patches joined into one burn

Of the 12 named urban fires, 8 have a patch of at least 50 destroyed buildings (the paper's urban conflagration), and in 8 of those 8 several patches of 20 or more sit within 75 m of each other and join into one larger burn. The 4 others (Angora, Grass Valley, Witch, Chimney Tops 2) never formed a patch of 50 in the per-building records.Patches: single-linkage groups of destroyed building centres at 30 m; groups of patches: 75 m groups holding at least 2 patches of ≥ 20. Named list = the frozen reference list of the definition study; same fire from several records shown once (Carlson or our record; outside surveys for Waldo Canyon and Lahaina).

Does the building layout tell which buildings were lost?

Network theory's first promise: maybe who is connected to whom explains losses better than how many neighbours a building has.

Building layout and network shape barely tell lost from surviving buildings inside a fire

Inside a fire, the layout of the buildings tells us little about which ones were lost: density and position alone score about 51, 50 and 53 in the three records (50 = coin flip). Adding network shape (group sizes, how many mutual neighbours, bridges, spreading strength) or a contagion-style spread on the network adds at most 1.3 points (at most 2.0 when each measure is scored within its own fire). What decides which buildings burn is mostly where the fire went (wind, embers, the fire front), which the building layout does not hold.Pre-registered tests (Holm over 9): network adds to density — does not add; spread adds beyond network — does not add; spread alone vs density — does not add. Model: L2 logistic, 10 fire-grouped folds; spread features = independent cascade on the kernel graph (β chosen inside training folds from 0.035–1; seeds uniform or edge-weighted). Fires with ≥ 10 lost and ≥ 10 not lost: Carlson 2002–22 345, Our 2002–26 record 432, CAL FIRE DINS 2013–25 109. Robustness (each measure as a within-fire z-score; values in the hovers): base AUC 55.9, 52.9, 48.2; largest gain over all main and robustness rows +2.0 points (upper 95% end +3.4).

How this panel was checked
  • Score is per fire (each fire counts once), only fires with at least 10 lost and 10 not lost buildings; held-out fires never used to fit or to pick the spread strength.
  • Intervals from resampling fires (2,000 draws); Holm adjustment over 3 records × 3 tests, as pre-registered.
  • Robustness: the same tests with each measure scored within its own fire (in the hovers); it changes the small gains but not the conclusion.
  • No fire attributes (wind, perimeter, severity) are used: only buildings standing before the fire.
